items.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006
items.q: I remember one time they had a big jam session and homecoming, Ellis Marsalis and Alvin Batiste and all of them was down.

ctx.x: So going back to college for a minute. You’re exploring all these things. You’re kind of doing that on your own apart from your education studies.

Oh yeah definitely. I remember one time they had a big jam session and homecoming, Ellis Marsalis and Alvin Batiste and all of them was down. And I was over at the library listening at John Cage and who else — oh it’s slipped my mind — well Stockhausen too but there was a classical composer, Ives, I was listening to Ives. And they thought I was listening to Burl Ives. I said, “Man, I was in the library listening to Ives.” “Oh you listen to Burl Ives? What’s wrong with you?” So I had to go along with it. So I came…
I’ll be darned. You have big ears.

items.title: Ellis Marsalis interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 7, 2020
items.q: I was thinking of Kidd Jordan.

ctx.x: I did. My mom thought I was crazy. I used to buy a lot of records. I ended up with a total of 376 long playing records which I eventually gave to the public library, which, you know, they’re probably still over there.

I don’t know exactly how to ask this question but what’s the most progressive music in jazz that you liked. I was thinking of Kidd Jordan. He called himself the last free man in New Orleans. And I wonder, so I’m going to change my question a little bit. Did you ever participate in what we might call free jazz?
I think I did once on a live concert. It was an alto saxophone player who came through New Orleans and I was in the rhythm section. And what was his name — he’s still on the faculty at Oberlin.
